title: Batching
summary:
Batching merges many independent work items into **one more efficient downstream operation**. It pays off whenever an operation has a **fixed cost per call**, such as a network round trip, request headers, a syscall, an `fsync` or a transaction commit, that a bigger payload amortises. With 5 ms overhead and 0.1 ms per item, 100 single calls take about 510 ms; one batch of 100 takes 15 ms.

Where does the batch come from?
1. **There is already a staging area** (a queue, a table of pending rows): take up to N items at once and send them together.
2. **There is none** (a client producing events): buffer in memory and flush when the buffer reaches **N items or K milliseconds**, whichever comes first. The timeout is mandatory; without it a quiet period leaves items stuck.

On the client it mostly cuts per-message overhead (Kafka producer `batch.size` and `linger.ms`, bulk inserts).

Costs to design for:
- **Latency:** an item can wait up to K ms; interactive paths use a tiny K.
- **Partial failure:** one bad item must not poison 99 good ones. Return per-item results, retry only the failures, and make processing [idempotent](#/sd/f/idempotency), since a retried batch may have partly succeeded.
- **Size caps** by count and bytes bound memory and timeouts.
- **Loss on crash:** an unflushed in-memory buffer disappears; buffer durably if items matter.
- **Ordering** within and across batches must be defined.

Batching also tames hot-key writes ([time bucket counter](#/sd/f/time-bucket-counter)) and makes [fanout](#/sd/f/fanout) affordable.

drills.q: Each call to a service has 5 ms of fixed overhead plus 0.1 ms per item. Items are sent sequentially, one call at a time. How many milliseconds does it take to send 1,000 items in batches of 100?
drills.explain: 10 calls x (5 + 100 x 0.1) = 10 x 15 = 150 ms. One item per call would be 1,000 x 5.1 = 5,100 ms. The saving comes from paying the 5 ms overhead 10 times instead of 1,000.

drills.q: A client buffers events and flushes when it has 50 events or 100 ms have passed since the first buffered event, whichever is first. Events arrive evenly at 400 per second. How many events does a typical flushed batch contain?
drills.explain: Filling 50 events would take 50 / 400 = 125 ms, which is longer than the 100 ms linger, so the timeout wins: 400 x 0.1 = 40 events. At higher rates the size cap triggers the flush instead.

drills.q: A batcher flushes only when it has 100 events. During the night the service sees 2 events per second. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Events are dropped; use a larger buffer
Events can wait about 50 seconds for a full batch; add a time-based flush so the buffer is sent after K milliseconds even if it is small
The downstream rejects small batches; always pad the batch
drills.explain: Size-only triggers starve at low traffic. 'Size or timeout' bounds latency to K regardless of load.

drills.q: A bulk write of 100 items returns an error for 3 items and success for 97. What is the right client behaviour?
options: Read the per-item results, retry only the 3 failures (or park the permanently invalid ones), and keep processing idempotent in case the retry repeats work
Retry the whole batch of 100 until it passes
drills.explain: Retrying everything duplicates the 97 successes unless writes are idempotent; dropping loses them. Per-item results let you retry precisely and isolate poison items.

drills.q: Put the life of a client-side batcher in order.
items: An event is added to the in-memory buffer; the linger timer starts if the buffer was empty
The buffer reaches N items or the timer fires
The buffer is swapped out and sent as one call downstream
Failed items are retried or dead-lettered; successes are acknowledged to their callers
drills.explain: Swap the buffer out so new events can accumulate while the call is in flight. Acknowledge each item individually; a batch result is really many results.

drills.q: Checkout authorises a card payment on a path with a p99 target of 200 ms. Someone proposes batching authorisations with a 500 ms linger to save calls to the processor. What do you say?
options: Good idea: fewer calls is always better
Yes, but only if the batch size is above 1,000
No: the linger alone exceeds the latency budget; batch only background work, or use a tiny linger that fits within the budget
Yes, since the processor charges per call
drills.explain: Batching trades latency for throughput. On an interactive, latency-budgeted path the linger time is added to every request; use it where waiting is acceptable.
